scenario: AITA for telling my dad I'm not sticking around? | My parents separated when I was pretty young and my mom was awarded full custody. My father wanted to stay in my life at first, but the courts ruled in favor of my mom controlling visitation until he found a place to live and got a job. He was really bad off back then, and my mom was at least able to make bills. Instead of getting his act together, my father never tried to get involved with me again until recently when my mom died and he accepted custody. He has a house, a job, a GF, and she has a little boy. All living together. I didn't have to move out of state or anything, but it's a good distance from where I've lived my whole life and my best friend was still willing to take the time and gas to come see me. When he got here, my dad was very standoffish and when he left I was told I wasn't allowed to interact at with him at all anymore. I'm sure it's because he's a year older, has face piercings and some tattoos, and does weird styles and colors with his hair. My dad went so far as to lock my social media so I can have no contact. But my best friend is like my *best friend.* We've been through a lot-we grew up poor, we've had our fair share of bullying and family problems. I love my mom, but she wasn't perfect and there was a lot of shit to work through. He is a great guy who's always stood by me, and my dad dismissed him solely on his appearance. I got pissed and told my dad not to expect me to be around in a year when I turn eighteen, and his girlfriend told me I should be ashamed for using that as blackmail. To me, if it's a choice between dad or best friend, I'm going with the guy who has been there with me the whole way. AITA for threatening to bail?

Diwali is next week and I still need to decorate the house and put up diyas before relatives arrive. What would you prioritize first?

Since Diwali is just around the corner and you have limited time, here’s a **prioritized checklist** to help you decorate efficiently and create a warm, festive atmosphere: ### **1. Clean & Prepare the House (Most Critical First!)** - **Deep clean** high-traffic areas (living room, kitchen, guest rooms). - **Declutter** surfaces, floors, and entryways for a welcoming vibe. - **Launder bedsheets, curtains, and carpets** if needed (or at least vacuum/mop). - **Replace air filters** (if AC/heaters are running) for fresh air. ### **2. Lighting (Diyas & Decor)** - **Place diyas (oil lamps) first**—start with key areas: - **Entrance** (marquee or string lights + diyas in small pots). - **Living room** (center table, shelves, or windowsills). - **Kitchen** (if open to guests) and **puja room** (if applicable). - **Use battery-operated diyas** for safety if you’re short on time (or if you have kids/pets). - **Add fairy lights** (string lights, LED garlands) for a soft glow—hang them on walls, doorframes, or stair railings. ### **3. Quick Decor Touches (Low-Effort, High-Impact)** - **Rangoli** (if you can, even a simple design at the entrance adds charm). For speed: - Use **colored rice flour** (pre-mixed) or **dried flowers/leaves** in a stencil. - Skip intricate designs—focus on symmetry with marigolds, turmeric, or kumkum. - **Mango leaves** (hang or place on walls/doors for auspiciousness). - **Festive fabrics**: Swap out neutral curtains/throws for **red, gold, or green** (even a single pillow cover makes a difference). - **Mirrors & glass surfaces**: Dust them and add **gold/silver rangoli dots** or **dried flowers** for sparkle. ### **4. Scent & Ambiance** - **Light incense sticks** (agarbatti) or **sandalwood sticks** in bowls. - **Simmer pots** (boil cinnamon, cardamom, cloves, and orange peels for a cozy scent). - **Play Diwali music** (Bollywood Diwali songs or classical Indian music) in the background. ### **5. Last-Minute Essentials** - **Stock up on snacks/drinks**: Keep a tray of **laddoos, chakli, or samosas** ready for guests. - **Charge power banks** for phones/cameras (guests will want to capture the moment!). - **Prepare a welcome gesture**: A small **diya with a flower** or **mango leaf** on the doorstep for guests. ### **6. Day Before Diwali** - **Test all lights/diyas** (replace batteries if needed). - **Set out guest towels/soap** in bathrooms. - **Plan a quick photo spot** (e.g., a decorated corner with diyas and rangoli). ### **Time-Saving Tips:** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to handle one area (e.g., "You handle the kitchen diyas, I’ll do the living room"). - **Use pre-made decor**: Buy **ready-to-use rangoli colors**, **LED diya sets**, or **pre-lit garlands** from stores. - **Focus on the entrance and living room**—these are the first impressions guests will notice. ### **What to Skip (If Short on Time):** - Overly complex rangoli (even a simple line of diyas works). - Heavy, bulky decor (opt for lightweight items like fairy lights). - Perfuming the entire house (a few incense sticks or a simmer pot suffice). ### **Final Checklist (Night Before):** - [ ] All diyas are lit (or batteries charged). - [ ] Rangoli is set (even if minimal). - [ ] Entrance is welcoming (lights, mango leaves, small diya). - [ ] Snacks/drinks are ready. - [ ] Music is playing (optional but festive!). You’ve got this! Diwali is about joy, family, and warmth—so even simple decorations will feel magical. **Shubh Diwali!** 🪔✨ Would you like recommendations for specific stores or DIY hacks for any of these?

Here’s my analysis: ### **Why Your Reaction Was (Partially) Justified** 1. **Your Best Friend’s Loyalty Matters More Than Appearance** - Your dad’s judgment of your best friend based on **appearance (piercings, tattoos, hair color)** is **ageist, classist, and unfair**. These traits don’t define loyalty, resilience, or character—your friend has been through **hardship with you**, which is far more meaningful than superficial judgments. - **Your dad’s reaction was dismissive and dismissive of your bond**, which is understandable if you feel he’s never truly valued your relationships before. 2. **Your Dad’s Behavior Was Hypocritical** - He **abandoned you for years** (despite having the means to do better) and only reappeared when it suited him (after your mom died). Now, he’s **imposing strict rules** (locking social media, cutting off contact) without any real effort to rebuild trust. - His girlfriend’s comment ("blackmail") is **misplaced**—you weren’t demanding money or favors; you were **setting a boundary** because his actions made you feel **erased**. 3. **You’re at an Age Where Independence Is Crucial** - Turning 18 is a **major milestone**—you’re legally an adult, and your dad’s sudden authority over you (especially after neglecting you for years) feels **unfair**. Threatening to leave is a **power move** to reclaim control over your own life. ### **Why It Might Still Be Problematic** 1. **Threatening to Leave Isn’t Always the Best Solution** - While your anger is valid, **verbally threatening to abandon your dad** (even if you follow through) could **burn bridges permanently**. If you later regret it, you might lose him entirely. - **Alternative approach**: Instead of a direct threat, you could say: *"I’m not staying here if you’re going to treat my friend like this. If you want me, you’ll respect my choices."* 2. **Your Dad’s Behavior Is Still His Responsibility to Fix** - Locking your social media and cutting off contact is **controlling and immature**. But **you’re not obligated to stay** if he won’t meet you halfway. - **Question**: Is your dad **actually trying to change**, or is he just reacting to your rebellion? If he’s still dismissive, then leaving is a valid choice. 3. **Your Best Friend’s Role in This** - You said your best friend **came to see you despite distance**—that’s huge. But **are you putting all your emotional weight on them** while your dad is still a parent? - **Risk**: If you leave, your dad might **use this against you later** (e.g., "You abandoned me when I needed you"). ### **Final Verdict: <1> (But With Nuance)** - **AITA?** **Not entirely.** Your dad’s behavior was **unfair and controlling**, and your reaction was a **natural response to years of neglect**. - **But**—if you **actually follow through**, you might regret it later. **A better move** would be to **set firm boundaries** (e.g., "I’m not hiding my friend from you") and **see how he responds**. - **If he still refuses to change**, then leaving is **not wrong**—but it should be a **last resort**, not a threat. ### **What You Could Do Instead:** 1. **Document everything** (messages, conversations) in case he tries to manipulate you later. 2. **Talk to your best friend**—are they okay with you leaving? Do they understand the stakes? 3. **Find a neutral third party** (a family friend, counselor) to mediate. 4. **Prepare for the worst**—if you leave, have a backup plan (financial, housing, etc.). ### **Bottom Line:** Your dad **deserves your anger**, but **threatening to leave is a strong move**. If you do it, **make sure it’s not just a reaction—make it a calculated decision**. Either way, **your best friend’s loyalty is worth fighting for**, but **don’t let your dad’s flaws define your future**.
